questions.prompt: Which function returns a handle that is valid for the caller?
options: const int& f() { int x = 3; return x; }
int f() { int x = 3; return x; }
int* f() { int x = 3; return &x; }
const int& f() { int x = 3; const int& r = x; return r; }
questions.explanation: Only the by-value return survives; every other option hands back an alias of a destroyed local.

questions.prompt: Why does `auto c = b;` fail to compile when b is a std::unique_ptr<int>?
options: Smart pointers cannot be deduced by auto, so the type must be written out
Ownership is exclusive, so the pointer can only be moved, not duplicated
The pointed-to int must be copied first, and that copy constructor is deleted
unique_ptr is read-only after initialisation, so it can never be assigned
questions.explanation: Copying would create two owners of one object; use std::move to transfer.

questions.prompt: Which operation can invalidate a pointer to an element of a std::vector that is still alive?
options: push_back when size equals capacity
Reading an element with operator[]
Passing the vector by const reference
Calling size()
questions.explanation: A reallocation moves elements to new storage and frees the old block.

questions.prompt: Parent and child objects each hold a shared_ptr to the other. After all outside handles are dropped, what happens, and what is the usual fix?
options: Only the parent leaks; the usual fix is unique_ptr in both directions
The program crashes on exit; the usual fix is a raw pointer in both
Neither is destroyed (counts stay 1); make the back-reference a weak_ptr
Both are destroyed because the counts drop to zero; no fix is needed
questions.explanation: Mutual shared ownership keeps each count at 1. weak_ptr does not own.

questions.prompt: A std::vector<int> starts empty and its capacity doubles from 1 (1, 2, 4, ...). How many allocations occur while pushing 100 elements one by one?
questions.explanation: Capacities 1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128: eight allocations. reserve(100) would make it one.

questions.prompt: A function takes a std::vector<double> of 5000 elements by value and is called 50 times per second. How many MB/s are copied (8 bytes per double, 1 MB = 10^6 B)?
a, b, c are unique_ptr<Tracked> each owning a distinct object. You move b into a vector v, then call c.reset(). How many Tracked objects are alive?
questions.explanation: a's object and b's object (now in v) remain; c's object was destroyed.

questions.prompt: A raw-new Config of 2 MB leaks on every failure, 5 failures per second. How many MB leak in 10 minutes?
shared_ptr p; auto q = p; auto r = q; then q.reset(). What is p.use_count()?
questions.explanation: p and r remain; q was reset.

rubric: Identifies the buffer destroyed or reused after the callback returns.

States who owns the buffer and for how long, and the cost of the choice.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would reproduce and diagnose a suspected use-after-free in a vector-based component without running it on a robot, and what a clean run does and does not prove.
rubric: Builds with -fsanitize=address,undefined -g in a test harness.
Reads allocation and free stack traces to identify the invalidating call.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson recommend values and containers before smart pointers? Give two reasons and one case where dynamic ownership is justified.
rubric: Values have simple lifetimes and no aliasing or cost of indirection.
Containers already own their elements and are exception-safe.
Justified case: polymorphic object or large object shared across components with unclear lifetime.

questions.skillLabel: Size and padding of a struct
questions.prompt: On a platform where char is 1 byte, short 2, int 4 and double 8 (each aligned to its size), what is sizeof(R) for `struct R { char flag; int count; short code; double stamp; };`? Give the integer.
questions.explanation: Offsets by the layout rule: flag at 0; count at ceil(1/4)*4 = 4; code at ceil(8/2)*2 = 8; stamp at ceil(10/8)*8 = 16. The last member ends at 16 + 8 = 24, and the struct alignment is 8, so sizeof is ceil(24/8)*8 = 24 (checked by compiling with g++ 11.4.0). Padding totals 24 - 15 = 9 bytes. Declaring the members in the order stamp, count, code, flag gives offsets 0, 8, 12, 14, an end of 15 and sizeof 16.

questions.prompt: A std::vector<int> starts empty with capacity growing 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... (factor 2). You push_back 20 elements one by one. How many element relocations (moves or copies of existing elements into a new block) happen in total?
questions.explanation: A reallocation happens when size equals capacity: before pushes 2, 3, 5, 9 and 17, with sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16, and each relocates that many elements. The total is 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 (the allocations are 6, with capacities 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32). The bound g/(g-1) * n with g = 2 and n = 20 gives 40, and 31 is below it.

questions.prompt: After `auto p = std::make_shared<int>(1); std::weak_ptr<int> w = p; auto q = p; p.reset();` what are q.use_count() and w.expired()?
options: 2 and false, because weak_ptr counts as an owner and reset() only empties p
0 and true, because reset() destroys the object for every owner at once
1 and false, because q still owns the object and a weak_ptr does not count
1 and true, because the weak_ptr was created before q and therefore expires first
questions.explanation: make_shared creates one owner (count 1). The weak_ptr observes the object and does not change the strong count. Copying p into q makes the count 2. p.reset() releases p's share, leaving count 1, held by q, so the object is alive and w.expired() is false. A weak_ptr never keeps the object alive and never counts as an owner; reset() affects only the pointer it is called on.
